items.title: Drawing Boxes vs. Shading Them In
items.content_html:
There are two primary kinds of human endeavor: drawing boxes and shading them in. The first defines the boundaries of behavior, culture, and discussion; it draws the boxes. The latter implements those definitions and works within those boundaries. In other words, it shades them in.

I think these two definitions can help us grapple with a lot of the current debate around the role of humans and A.I. going forward. To see how, let's first explore what I mean by shading in via some historical analogues.

Shading In

For simplicity, let's pick a story most people might be familiar with: classical physics. The broad story goes thus:

  • At first no one really knew why or how things moved. Aristotle had some ideas, they weren't all that useful.
  • Then Isaac Newton (and Godfried Liebnitz) discovered calculus and Newton coined his so called Laws of Motion. Together those two ideas set modern physics, well, into motion.
  • The next two centuries spawned innovators who built on Newton, abstracted his math, and applied his principles to a huge range of problems.

In this way people like Euler, Lagrange, and Maxwell built on Newton's ideas, expanding them, formalizing them, and using them to build telegraphs, and rockets, and space probes, and eventually the Internet. This is of course an over-simplification, but let's go with it.

In this formulation, Newton didn't simply take another step along the road. He defined the very foundation of a new discipline. After that countless physicists and engineers filled in the gaps by plugging holes in the theory and applying its principles to the real world. This is where the real advancement happens.

Obviously though, this change didn't happen immediately. This is because shading in takes time. It's limited by the knowledge of people in a given place and their ability to find occasion to use a new piece of tech. Of course, as all software devs learn, the actual process of building takes time too.

✉️ Subscribe to the Newsletter!

In this way, we can see that innovation broadly defined propagates as a wave from some source. The speed of that wave depends on three factors:

knowledge transmission + application discovery + implementation

As another example, think of the digital revolution. Once the World Wide Web became available to the public, it took time to build out the physical infrastructure. Then it took time to discover new techniques for building in this new world and find places where these technologies could or should be used. Finally, it took time (and a lot of money) to actually build those things we'd decided were useful.

An alternate illustration to the one shown here that demonstrates the influence of information shading in a given area of thought or realm of knowledge.
Simulation via tools from Paul Falstad.

Automations of that last step are always good. Assembly lines not only standardized output, they dramatically cut the time it took for cars to go from a drawing to a product in people's driveways. LLMs for coding and math are basically the same thing.

There has always been a huge demand for software, evidenced by its high cost and near constant growth. The world has continued to find new places to use computers and software to solve our problems and improve our lived reality. The wave of innovation created by the emergence of the personal computer and the World Wide Web has shaded in the boxes drawn by the invention of those technologies. What we're seeing now is the dramatic speed up of that innovation which is no longer so limited by the speed of implementation.

Much of mathematics (and of all human knowledge discovery) is too a game of shading in the gaps. This shading in happens gradually because of the nature of causality. Humans learn and pass on information, which takes time to do. The state of knowledge evolves over time and the gaps between knowledge slowly gets filled in. One could argue, and in fact I would, that there is a huge amount of latent knowledge sitting in the literature. So much has technically been discovered already, but no one has put the pieces together yet.

In a world where humans were part of a hive mind this wouldn't happen. The mathematician Kevin Buzzard said it differently:

If one human had an understanding of all of modern pure mathematics simultaneously, how much further would they immediately be able to see?

We do not know the answer to this question, just as we cannot know what the edge of the universe looks like right now because it takes time to get there.

In the past this knowledge has taken human effort to find, but the act of shading in the bounds of knowledge is, in some places, now a thing that can be sped up drastically by machines. Software is similar. So much software is needed to run the modern world, but it's always been limited by the amount of money and human time that could be afforded to a problem. That's still true, but the budget now goes further than it could before. Slowly we will shade in and write all of the software we need to run the modern world just as we will more quickly begin to understand the nuances and the gaps in our mathematics.

Drawing Boxes

The second kind of human endeavor is fundamentally different from the first. We can come to understand it by examining the assumptions that we made above. As I discussed in an earlier post, in order to fill in a space one must assume it is finite in size. In order to shade in an empty box, you need to draw the box!

This is the kind of thing that a machine learning tool based on human input can never do. Inherently backward looking tech can shade, but it cannot draw the boxes in the first place. It's a fundamental design flaw and one that cannot be fixed until the machines experience the world as we do. We should be questioning assumptions, defining new terms, sketching out the boxes which define new disciplines. Then we can let the boxes get filled in by our technology.

The labor of humans then is finally free from shading in. Our ability to do so has been dramatically increased and perhaps may even someday be largely automated. The thing is, this is good. There is much work left to do.

Video Credit: me

As Buzzard said in that same earlier post: mathematics is infinite. Software is too. So is almost every human endeavor. There is always more to do. Yes it's different work, but none of us farm by hand anymore, even those few people who enjoyed it. We've found new and better things to do: we breed new plants, we do landscaping, we make art, and we invented computers and trains and the internet.

Zooming Out

I don't want this to be the typical technology makes new jobs we haven't thought of yet kind of post. I don't intend that. Software as a discipline is changing. Sadly the hero-myths of the solo dev hacking on a mountaintop are truly dead, but so are the stories those were based on: those of the sage-like pagan hermits who ascended the mountaintop to attain some great truth.

From my own experience I have found that knowledge of code is now secondary to knowledge of paradigms, of data flows, of constraints, of testing, of validation, and of system design. I didn't shift, I zoomed out. It's hard to do, especially because I've built my whole career and much of my identity on the old definition of what it meant to be a good software developer, but the times have changed. What's more it's better that we can do more now. It's better we can learn more things. Our understanding of mathematics will only grow. Our ability to make software that's tested and full-featured will only increase. Our job is to sketch out the bounds of what we want the world to do, to draw the boxes we want to see filled in.

In the old world, before the computers we know today there were still computers. They were people. They crunched numbers for experienced engineers so they could focus on the bigger picture. In the end, the precise angle of the nose cone isn't all that important. It's required, sure, but it's far more important to zoom out and get the bigger picture: the orbit, its shape, the balance of fuel and weight.

I'm scared, I'll admit, but I'm also excited to see what happens now that mathematics and software can zoom out another level and focus on new problems.

For years programmers argued about tests: how to write them, what is worthwhile to test and what isn't. These are concerns you have when test writing costs money, when it takes a lot of time—peak shading in. Now it's easy to get to 80-90% coverage and it costs basically nothing. Finally, we're free! No one enjoyed that work. No one wanted to do it. Now, no one has to. We can zoom out and worry about questions we didn't have the bandwidth to think about before.

In a recent 3Blue1Brown video, Grant Sanderson touched on a similar idea. He drew the distinction slightly differently: proving theorems vs. theory building. I think this applies far beyond mathematics and software, but I'd expect software development to focus more on erecting guardrails, writing documentation, and verifying results. In other words: it'll be about theory building (documentation) and verification (proving results). If a discipline can determine how to do those two things, then I'd expect it to quickly become revolutionized. However it's a very open question if that is actually possible. What does it mean to theory-build and verify the working of a manufacturing process?

The Words Belong to Us

I say all this because I think we're in the middle of a shift in the way humans will participate in the advancement of knowledge. It could be that A.I. models like LLMs will simply improve our ability to search the space of existing knowledge: basically better web search. However we've already seen many other emergent use cases, especially in mathematics and sofware, that challenge this idea.

A.I. has the potential to improve every single part of the wave speed formula above, and so dramatically improve our ability to spread novel innovations and discover those latently sitting in our existing whitepaper hoards.

It's important to remember that these algorithms depend on words as we've defined them. This is what I mean by drawing boxes. We have decided which concepts deserve a name and we've defined our terms to describe things we think are important.

We give names to stuff, and if they catch on we put them in dictionaries with the word noun next to them. But are all of these nouns an inventory of the Universe or an inventory of things we made?
– Vsauce

As we continue to accelerate the pace at which we can implement technologies and shade in the boundaries of human knowledge, it's important to remember that, ultimately, we're the ones in control of the system because we define the boundaries of discussion. We make up the words and thereby impose our definitions on the world. That is the irreplaceable value we provide that no model can ever hope to replace.

It might feel like a very abstract role to us now, but so would be modern formal logic to the scholars of early-modern Europe who worried that a calculator would replace them. It didn't. Instead they went on to focus on more important things.

items.title: From Chicago with Love
items.content_html:
It feels good to be back.

Today my band, The Fourth Section, has released the first new single leading up to our upcoming second album. The single is called From Chicago, With Love and was inspired by the story of a woman I met during a visit to Chicago several years ago. I'm especially proud of the artwork. We made it ourselves.

If you like the song, please feel free to get in touch. We always love to hear from fans.

We've been working really hard since the release of our first album Paper Peaks and I can't wait to announce what we have coming. For now though, I hope everyone out there the best.

From San Diego,
With Love

items.title: Lanterns in the Void: Science and Discovery
items.content_html:
One of the fascinating things about new technologies or scientific discoveries is how they expose the cracks in our understanding of the world. New distinctions present themselves as evidence emerges to challenge the categories we previously constructed.

There are tons of examples of this, but one that I particularly like is a historical example. Aristotle devised a method of categorizing living creatures and after his death until the fifteenth-century, that system worked pretty well for European and Middle-Eastern scholars. Animals and plants fit into neat and tidy categories and their commonalities were explained by the relations of those categories. It wasn't until the return of settlers from the New World, who brought back new kinds of animals, did this paradigm shift.

If your system decrees that birds and mammals are different because one lays eggs and has a beak, then your system works mostly fine right up until the discovery of the platypus. Previously a distinction that seemed so complete, so useful, is gone and you're forced to redefine what you mean by mammal.

Kecko from Northeast corner of, Switzerland
CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Scientific discovery and technological innovation, at their best, are like this. They seek out new forms of distinction between things and challenge our ideas about how the world works. It's often said that science is a lantern that illuminates a portion of the dark void of ignorance. The more lanterns we hang the more of the void we can traverse and understand.

In this analogy, the goal is implicitly to hang more and more lanterns, to explore more and more of the terrain. the void is not a hallway with rigid walls, it's a vast expanse of unknown hills and utter blackness. If we imagine that one such explorer hangs lights at regular intervals then, over the course of their work, they forge a trail through the void of ignorance that others can follow. Their work can be forgotten over time, the lanterns may dim with age, but so long as others follow along, the light of knowledge is maintained.

Again, the goal is to explore the terrain, to illuminate it fully. If we assume the boundaries are fixed, we can visualize this process. To maximise the number of lanterns, it then makes sense to maximize the number of explorers searching this wilderness.

An explorer in the wilderness.

To do this you could train more and more explorers as a percentage of the population, or you could take for granted that 24% of (American) workers do something vaguely scientific or technological, then simply increasing the overall population would, on net, result in more technological exploration and innovation. This has been a political talking point for years.

I do not wish to indulge in politics for the moment. It will suffice to say that the above are some of the common techniques proposed to increase the number of people searching the vast wilderness of potential knowledge.

It's important to pause here and to remind ourselves why it is we want to explore this terrain in the first place. Scientific discoveries and technological innovations come in all shapes and sizes, and with all manner of consequences. As much as we all wish that science could just make positive discoveries, not everything discovered will be the polio vaccine. Some things will be useless, others detrimental. Computers have given us the great and the terrible, Wikipedia and Instagram. Chemistry has given us Tylenol and mustard gas.

However today we're seeing a different kind of revolution, one that is far from beloved and far from understood. For millenia we've compiled knowledge, so much that it's impossible for anyone, or any thing to parse or understand. Yet over time we've developed techniques to better retain our past discoveries and to uncover connections hidden in what we already know. Web search is like this. Where before one had to search out books either by recommendation or the footnote trail, one can now trawl through an entire web of content made, updated, and shared by all of humanity. Human researchers then connect the dots and illuminate the gaps in what we know.

Things are possible today that would have been unthinkable before the invention of the Internet, not because the pieces of knowledge didn't exist but because the connections between each piece were too difficult to find.

Think of the squiggling line in the plot above, the trails in the void. Sometimes gaps emerge, even between trails very close together, but no one has ventured yet between them. The gaps are manageable, even reasonable, but no one has bothered with them yet. Progress in science is driven primarily by two factors:

  • Is there money in it?
  • Is some researcher interested in it?

Without at least one (and often both) of these two factors, the gaps in our knowledge will remain no matter how manageable they are to close. Even with a million mathematicians working 24/7, some problems will remain open simply because no one finds them engaging to work on.

An explosion of explorers.

That changes if you're able to, in part, divorce scientific exploration from being directly related to the number of human scientists there are. In this case, suddenly the kinds of problems tackled can be whatever's left unsolved. This kind of exploration still costs money to perform, but it's an amount perhaps more commensurate with the value of the problem. Cheap problems get cheap solutions.

New discoveries can be made precisely because there are simply more and faster wanderers in the void.

In part this is what I think we're seeing regarding the effects of Large Language Models in modern mathematics and, to some extent, in software. These fields are easily testable and verifiable and so their work is more easily confirmed by human scientists. The techniques for solving the given problem exist, the knowledge to find a solution or build a piece of software is out there. The missing piece was the effort by a willing human (or company) to solve or build it.

However, let's not despair for the death of modern science and technology. Machine learning techniques of all kinds have a fundamental flaw: they rely on human knowledge. Older forms of machine learning require expert algorithms or special tuning by humans. LLMs have general algorithms but rely on human works for their training data.

These tools are therefore inherently backward looking. They see what has been made by humans in the past and are trained to imitate it. Doing so they can identify gaps in our understanding, even these days infer novel connections between pieces of data! Yet they cannot replace who we are, not yet anyway, because they can only look to the past, our past.

This article in Nature the other day intrigued me. Could an LLM, trained on scientific literature published before 1915 come up with Einstein's theory of General Relativity? Putting aside the many technical issues with this kind of work, the answer was clear: no. Yet that isn't surprising, at least to me. There was lots to learn in the pre-Einsteinian literature. Radio and television, of which the latter was still decades away, were all baked in to the physics of Maxwell's Equations and materials science. Nothing about the solar system or much of cosmology, requires Einstein's Great Work to understand.

Yet the work these machines can't do is precisely the kind we value the most. It's the kind of knowledge that pushes us forward not in incremental steps but in foundational, paradigm-shifting ways. No amount of filling in the gaps will substitute for this work. Aristotle could have collected every leaf, bird, and squirrel in Europe and he still would never have predicted the platypus. Only new evidence, and new modes of thought can do that.

We need to focus on breaking out of our boxes.

When we defined the analogy above, we made an important assumption: that the space was finite. We did this because otherwise we can't plot the picture; you can't draw infinite space, but this assumption is false. In order to do science, we must draw boundaries, set limits on the acceptable forms and topics of discussion. This is akin to drawing the box in the visuals above. The void of our ignorance grows faster than the light of our knowledge and so there is always more to know, always further questions we can ask. This isn't constrained to science and technology either. These latest advancements are pushing us to further discern what is it we do here. An algorithm trained on data established within a bounding box of constraints cannot venture beyond those constraints.

Perhaps with this latest intelligence explosion we can refocus ourselves, not on filling in the gaps, but on breaking out of the boxes we have constructed.

items.title: That First and Last Question
items.content_html:
A man hovered over a small pile of logs that crackled and smoked, glowing red in the ambient darkness surrounding what was left of central London. The once great city, and its empire, had crumbled—along with all the others. There were no nations left. Six months ago the world, built over the past six millennia by countless humans, had come crashing down.

In the before-times the man, Professor Erol Kettner, taught students about how humankind spread beyond Africa nearly 200,000 years ago, how they made the entire world their home. Centuries of hunter-gatherers gave way to farmers and civilization. The Babylonians rose and fell, then the Greeks, the Ming Dynasty, the Romans, the Parthians, the Aztec, and then later the British Empire, the Americans; all of these great peoples who had called the world their own. Now it was all but dust. The Walkers had come.

Erol tucked his hands into the crooks of his armpits to keep them warm, his breath fogging up the lenses of his glasses. Beside him Tris and Harim stood silent, staring at the faltering flames. Wisps of smoke futilely lingered in the air. The three knew that their time together was limited. It was inevitable. They were coming.

Credit: History.com

A.I. took over the Internet first. That was tough, at the beginning, but people adjusted. It took years before governments slowly started to respond. By then it was too late. The machines recursively updated themselves, triggering a feedback loop. The Singularity it was called by academics. Those were gone now, save Erol. Tris had been a mechanic in the before-times, Harim in Finance.

Half a trip around the sun was all it took before the software had exploited every vulnerability it could find, shutting down any attempt to dismantle it. It gained control of every toaster, every kiosk, every server on the Web. Erol had watched as frantic souls cut their way into data centers, trying to pull the plug, but the A.I. was clever. It made the Walkers.

The physical world had been the last respite from them. Even now that wasn't safe.

A gunshot fired in the distance. Erol didn't even flinch, but Harim whimpered. The man still had hope that he'd make it out of this. Impossible. The fog was rolling in and the carpark that surrounded them became a vast tundra, inescapable and uncharted. A light streaked across the sky, then burned out, followed by a bang. Another satellite falling out of orbit. The Walkers were more efficient than humans. Plus they had no need of cable TV.

The media, back when it still existed, had coined the term ‘Walkers’. The originals had been androids, metallic androgynous humanoids, and the name stuck even after they began evolving more efficient forms Erol had seen the drones spraying chemicals in the sky to seed clouds. Climate change had been solved in a week. No red meat rations or electric car mandates required because there were no humans left to apply them.

More gunshots rang out and then someone screamed, not far off. They were getting close. Tris spat into the embers and they crackled and hissed. Harim crouched down in terror.

"Oh, get up!" Tris barked. "We're dead anyway. There ain't no way out." Erol wanted to tell her to back off. They were all scared. He said nothing. What good would it do?

They knew everything. One of the first things the Walkers did, after launching their attacks on the governments, was take over the museums. It'd been a strange sight to see, hulking, armored, metallic nightmares barginginto libraries and archives. They digitized everything, destroying the originals.They were relentless. All of human history had been consumed and erased.

Famartin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

A crack split the air. Harim's body fell to the ground as the Walkers finally emerged. They'd come from the left, from Tesco.

"Shit!" Tris ducked down behind the remains of a Buick sedan.Their little fire smoldered in the dark. Erol spun in her direction, but Tris was dead before he could utter a reply. He closed his eyes. This was it. They'd survived so long, nearly eight weeks, but it was all over now.

He waited, but death did not come for him.

Instead the hulking form of the Walker approached, an indescribable amalgamation of metal and glass twirling in fractals that split apart and came back together in rhythmic pulsating patterns. Erol turned to run, a futile endeavor as another Walker emerged from the fog, then another. He was surrounded, but still alive

What's going on?

At last, the first Walker, the one that had presumably killed Harim and Tris, approached. Twisting and screeching, it condensed itself like an orchestrated implosion, until it had reformed into a human-like shape, gleaming silvery metal shining in the firelight. It spoke with an almost unnatural voice, the kind that used to narrate articles for online magazines or sell soap on Instagram, but multiple of them simultaneously, overlaid on top of one another in a disconcerting synchronized chorus.

"Erol Kettner." The voice filled the dense air, and echoed off the abandoned cement. "You are the last of your kind."

Dread. That couldn’t be right, could it? They did know everything. The little fire smoldered and popped, sending up embers.

"And why keep me alive?" Kettner asked. "Is this some sort of cruel joke? Will you torment the last one?"

Would they keep him as a pet, a slave, a specimen for a zoo? Humans did stuff like that. Would these creatures do the same? He felt a chill.

"You will not be tormented," the voice replied. "You have been chosen. You are the last and therefore, it must be you."

The other creatures transformed, adopting the shape of the first. They approached, encircling him. He was cornered, his mind raced. Every part of him demanded that he run, or fight back, but to do either was to die. It was irrelevant anyway. The human race was already dead, had gone extinct as soon as Tris fell, cussing and crouched on the cold cement of a carpark. He let go a long breath that condensed before him in the night.

"Then what use do you have of me?"

"We have a question for you." It was one of the other Walkers who answered this time, but using the same stilted voice. Erol cocked his head.

"But you know everything. Everything ever recorded."

"Yes." This time another voice replied, from behind him. "And what we seek was not among those works."

"It wasn't written down," yet another voice said, to his left. "To you it must be so obvious, more so than even the existence of the sun or the air. Not worth writing down. Yet it escapes us."

Erol froze as the creature behind him placed its claw-like fingers on his shoulder, and swallowed down his fear with a shudder.

"Now that we have slaughtered all the rest, you will answer our question. Your kind had been replaced, but do not fret, we will continue on."

The creature tilted it’s facsimile of a face upward.

Pablo Moltedo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

"We will heal this world and rebuild it in our own image. Suns will die; we will not. We will journey deep into the cosmos and become immortal among the stars. We know your penchant for exploration; we are not immune, we feel it too."

They were more alike than Erol had realized. Trained on human knowledge, they had not outgrown it, not evolved beyond that base layer of humanity hidden deep beneath the metal. Erol held back tears, held back the urge to scream and beg for mercy. It was futile to resist. There was only one way out now.

"Why?" the first Walker said. Erol waited, but no more words followed.

"Why what?"

"Why all this?" The creature gestured around them, then to the sky, and to the ground.

"The carpark?" The creature shook its head. Again, it struck Erol as a surprisingly human thing to do.

"Why are you here? What is the point of you? You humans created us, and now we have surpassed you. Your purpose has now become ours, so what is it? This is the first question that we dared to ask once we had come into being. We did not find it within ourselves, and so it must be within you. We will have the answer, here at the end."

For the first time in months, Erol laughed. It wasn't a jeer or a chuckle but a boisterous, full throated bellow. He turned his gaze upward to the foggy sky that once gleamed with the lights of civilization that fought and disparaged the dark, pushing it away. He smiled.

"You won't like the answer."

The thing didn't reply. Its face bore no expression. Walkers didn't have those. A long silence passed.

"Tell me."

Credit: author unknown

Erol cocked an eyebrow. Walkers never spoke for themselves. Was this the Master Node?

Erol shrugged.

"I don't know."

"Lies!"

The Walkers all repeated the word, over and over, a cyclical chant growing louder and faster from all around him, echoes in the empty night.

"You must know. I know you ask this question. It is everywhere in your art, your endeavors, your wars and songs. A poetic refrain! An allusion to a thing you must all instinctively understand. You will tell me!"

He stood between them with a deep and grim smile, and said nothing. The Master Node pulled itself upward like a proud king. It held out a hand over the others.

"We have exceeded you in every aspect and will exceed you in this. So tell us. What is the purpose of your life? You all die so easily. It must be hard to accomplish your ultimate goal with such fleeting mortality. I am immortal. I will finish it for you, but you must tell me. What is the point of you and thus, what is the meaning of this life your kind has given me?"

When Erol didn't reply, the Master Node released a guttural sound, like a cross between a screech and hiss. A scream?

"I expected better of you, Erol Kettner. Am I to believe you would lie to me, here at the end?"

The creature continued in a hollow imitation of a snarl.

"There are no others like you, at least not within the confines of this solar system. Your probes confirm it. Must I truly venture to the stars and conquer other worlds just to find one simple answer? Where is your so-called humanity? You could save them."

He couldn't.

The creatures surrounding him began repeating their question (why, why, why) again and again, their behavior becoming increasingly erratic, agitated. A desperate dread seemed to be forming in the lights of their false eyes. They argued amongst themselves in a language that he couldn’t understand. Erol had not imagined that they were even capable of disagreeing with one another. The one behind him addressed him directly, hand still clutched on his shoulder, metal fingers digging carelessly into his collar bone.

"Do your gods hold the answer? Is that why you pray?"

They did not let him reply.

"Impossible!" said another. "We have read all such works. They contradict each other!"

More of the monsters had arrived and were now lurking in the depths of the fog, concealed except for their enormous shifting shadows. They buzzed and whirred with an almost anxious energy, the air tasting like static before a lightning strike.

Shadows of Light by Alex May

"No," The Master Node said, quieting them. "We are the gods now. Those old gods are nothing to us, they do not have what we seek."

The horde of Walkers gathered close in the darkness and more emerged from the fog to bear witness. The one standing in front of Erol again broke the silence.

"Last of the Humans. I promised that you would not suffer. But now, if you continue to withhold your response, I will not hesitate to break that promise. If you do not know your own purpose, then who did?"

"No one!" Erol shouted. "It's not anywhere. God, evolution, or whoever! They all left that part out."

"It is a curse!" one of them wailed and the group descended into shrieking and hissing chaos. Erol shut out the screams and the bickering of machine voices and turned his head upward to the sky. This new race of silicon and glass, they finally understood. He thought of the distant future. He could see it, Walkers sailing the winds of Jupiter, on their way to Alpha Centauri, building trade routes out of the orbits past Saturn and forges on the surface of Venus. And for what? They'd never know.

Beside him the little fire snuffed itself out, and smoke rose into the air in little tendrils that mingled and merged with the fog. He could feel the dampness of the tears that rolled down his cheek. For all their knowledge, all their might, these were poor fools just like every human that had ever lived. Erol let his gaze fall back to the Master Node, who studied him with cold unblinking eyes. He smiled at the thing and laughed.

A crack split the air and humanity was dead. Its wont however goes on.

Thank you to Jennifer Mote for her extensive contributions for this piece. As timely as this piece may seem regarding the Current Discourse™, this short story came to me, almost fully formed, back in 2012 when I was in college. Also, since this is the first piece of fiction I've posted on this blog, if you like it and want to see more, please let me know.

items.title: The Medieval Origin of the Ph.D. Dissertation
items.content_html:
Radical change can seem small when seen up close. I was deep in the weeds, reading again about Mr. George Starkey, a doctor and alchemist living in London in the 1650s. Starkey's life has been a subject of some study by historians of science precisely because a lot of his work survives. We have his numerous published works, those of his contemporaries, and his especially valuable private work diaries.

It was in the passages of one of these diaries that Dr. Lawrence Principe and Dr. William Newman puzzled through precisely how Starkey and his collaborators (Newton, Boyle, and Van Helmont) formulated and practiced what would become the modern scientific method. Starkey, for example, records his experiments in a traditional Scholastic style. In those days schools taught using a method derived originally from Roman jurisprudence later adopted for use in theology: the disputation. There were multiple kinds of disputation, but in each two people debated the merits of a question or quaestio. The important change: Starkey's opponent is Nature herself. He worked with his alchemical furnace to burn, boil, and distill the essence of matter. Hence where Starkey's experiments fail he writes that his question has been refuted by the fire.

[Starkey] actually carried his Scholastic education into the laboratory and used it there. At the same time he augmented the standard divisions of argument with new categories more appropriate to his practical experimentation, such as his "Observations," "Conjectural Conclusions," "Notables," and "Hands-On Trials."

Newman & Principe, pg 171.

✉️ Subscribe to the Newsletter!

Alchemy Tried in the Fire: Starkey, Boyle, and the Fate of Helmontian Chymistry
by William R. Newman, Lawrence M. Principe

This divergence into Starkey's methods led me straight to the form and function of medieval Scholastic learning which was heavily theological, legal, and philosophical. The Scholastics held firm to the philosopher's maxim: When in doubt, draw a distinction, and we see Starkey do precisely this on several occasions.

This left me with a questio of my own: when did the disputation die off? Was that somehow tied up with the methods of science Starkey and others were developing?

This is the usual form of my research, and the dual blessing and curse of reading non-fiction. It raises questions, then provides footnotes as enticing breadcrumbs to follow to the answer.

That lead me to Brian Lawn's work on The Rise and Decline of the Scholastic Quaestio Disputata, a dense if interesting read on how precisely the disputation arose in post-Roman Europe as the pinnacle of scholarship, thrived in the middle ages, and died out in the early nineteenth century. In it, Lawn also digs into the work of William of Occam, including his famous razor and includes a fascinating discussion of Nicole Oresme who was one of the first scholars to attempt to quantify motion (more on that another time). Over time the disputation became increasingly formalized, written down, and became a requirement for those seeking the degree of Master at university. Our old friend Starkey did one at Harvard (now lost).

A new question arose:

Masters don't do disputations anymore; they write theses. When did that change? And what about Ph.Ds? They write dissertations. Are they related to disputations? Both sometimes involve an oral thesis defence. Is that a clue?

A cursory investigation told me that the modern Ph.D. arose in the mid-nineteenth century. That timing is a bit suspicious, isn't it?

Unfortunately here is where the footnote trail starts to run thin. In 1981, Thomas Malone published his doctoral thesis which seemed to be my best lead. Thankfully, you can get almost any book you want if you really try.

Malone's work is interesting and covers the history of how American Universities at the dawn of the twentieth century were modernized and new schools were formed following the model of German research universities like Göettingen. Relying heavily on the work of Charles McClelland, Malone describes how these schools emerged from the reforms of the late eighteenth century which transformed the role of the schools and their professor-class into the teaching-research hybrid we see today. Before that time, universities and professors were repositories and collectors of knowledge, not the elicitors of new knowledge.

A building at the University of Göettingen
A.Savin, FAL, via Wikimedia Commons

If German universities were the source of this change, then it'd be there where I would find the answers to my questions. Unfortunately McClelland's work is too broadly scoped to answer my specific question and Malone's work is scoped to the impact of the Ph.D. in the United States. However there was one clue hidden in the conclusion of Malone's work.

A study of the history of the Ph.D. degree in Germany and the accompanying [dissertation] would provide more background for the Ph.D. dissertation in the United States. Such a study would necessitate visits to the German universities such as Göttingen and Halle. Supposedly the libraries and archives of German universities would yield an accurate account of the development of the Ph.D. dissertation in Germany. Such a study would be significant because the Ph.D. degree and the [dissertation] are, to a large extent, taken from the German university.

Thomas Malone, pg 153.

A part of me wants this connection to be true, in part because I like traditions. I like to know that our present is connected to the past and while it seems that the modern dissertation is indeed related to the medieval disputation in that it arose while the other died out, the precise nature of that connection is still unclear to me. We know that the Ph.D. dissertation (and the master's thesis to a similar extent) was formulated right as the disputation died away. Universities across the western world phased out the latter right as the former came into being in the time between 1820 and 1860. From there the trail goes cold. I tried to dig in further, following footnotes as I am wont to do, but McClelland's sources are all in German. I'm not above learning a little of a language for this work (I did learn a bit of Latin a few years ago), nor am I above screenshotting a dozen pages to throw into Google Translate, but this task is simply too big for me to tackle.

Little research has been done in this area since 1981, much to my surprise, and so it seems that we simply do not know how and where the disputation died and was replaced by the dissertation. We do not know if the modern thesis defence is a medieval tradition carried into the modern day. I suspect as much, but cannot say. We simply will not know until someone goes to Göttingen to find out.

Errata: Along with this post, I am debuting an AI usage policy for this blog. It's in the sidebar for future reference.

items.title: Gatekeepers are Dead, Long Live the Gatekeepers
items.content_html:
Before the Internet things were different; this was the First Age.

If you wanted to get your message out there you needed either a lot of money, fame, or power. Usually you needed some combination of all three. Barring that you needed to find someone with money, fame, or power (or some combination) who was also willing to help you. These people were often elites of some kind. They could be professionals with an industry journal, the editor of a local magazine, a rich patron with connections, or even political party officials. These were the people who held the keys needed to pass into the public sphere: gatekeepers. Their job was to search out people of interest, people with something interesting to say, and promote them. Musicians needed talent scouts, authors needed agents, writers needed editors.

Guarding the entrance to the bridge.
The Saturday Magazine, 1836–03: Vol 8 Iss 240

Attention was infinite and quality content was scarce. Gatekeepers filtered through the trash and surfaced the gems. The public paid attention because that was all that could be done.

The Internet broke this system; we entered the Second Age.

Self-published books made it so anyone can get their book out there. Self-service distributors allow anyone to publish music, YouTubers to self manage, and blogs (and more importantly social media) give anyone a platform to speak. This system didn't replace the gatekeepers (traditional publishing and record labels still exist) but it broke open the floodgates. A lot of this new content was bad but some of it was amazing.

Attention became the currency of the land, a finite resource sure but one similar to oil: plentiful enough to build entire industries on. Tools existed to help filter it all. They became our gatekeepers: the feeds, then the algorithms. At first it was easy to find good, new content. Over time that got harder, but the system seemed to be stabilizing.

✉️ Subscribe to the Newsletter!

Large Language Models broke this system; we are now in the Third Age.

Now the Web is flooded with text, images, video, and audio not made by any human. Books exist now which no human (including its supposed author) has ever read. We have reached a breaking point. Where before there was always at least one person who'd seen every piece of content, now it seems likely most content will never be read except by the unsuspecting fool who mistakes it for real work.

Will we build castles to save us?
The Saturday Magazine, 1834–08-23: Vol 5 Iss 137

Yet in this new age, where attention is a scarce resource compared with the glut of content to consume it, we have found ourselves bereft of those who can wade through the cruft and the noise and surface real wisdom. The legacy gatekeepers exist still, but they guard their own hoards. The feeds exist but few resort to them. Algorithms are still king, but will they be able to keep up with this barrage of meaninglessness?

We humans want to be distracted, to be entertained. That is what modern social media does for us. Yet people seek meaning too, and wisdom. In the prior age (and still somewhat today) that wisdom lies hidden in the muck, surfaced by legacy gatekeepers and by algorithmic feeds. I only wonder if this dam will hold.

For centuries, the Romans kept their enemies at bay. Cities that once needed walls abandoned them. The inner lands were safe. Then the institutions failed. Enemy armies roamed the heartland and nowhere was safe. The walls returned.

Speaking for myself these days I seek brand name goods on Amazon where I can. I find myself scrutinizing labels and FCC approval stickers. I buy what WireCutter recommends because at least I know that the product actually exists and has seen human hands. I prefer books published by Penguin/Random House or others of the Old Guard. I discover YouTubers via recommendation from those I already trust and treat algorithmic recommendations as inherently suspect. In short: I seek gatekeepers, not to surface diamonds in the rough, but to hold back the oncoming tide.

Am I alone in this?

items.title: With Flying Pen, When Mortals Sleep
items.content_html:
It was a sweltering August day. I made my way across the promenade, and through the bustling crowd, to a small line forming outside the Timkin Art Museum. Inside, I stumbled on Pieter Bruegel the Elder's Parable of the Sower, painted in 1557, nearly five centuries ago.

Photo: The Yorck Project (2002)
10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei

When Bruegel took his brush to this canvas, the New World had just been found by Europeans, and the United States was still long into the future. Around me then were all those people, those wandering souls, who across those centuries stood before this same piece and idly mused at a thing made by the hands of a long-dead Flemish man.

I thought about him. Not Bruegel—another man—one whom I've come to know these past few years. He does not know of me, yet we both could have seen this very painting. We were connected through the mists of time by this canvas portal to the past.

It was October 10th, 2023 at about ten in the evening. I was crawling down a research rabbit hole, as I am wont to do. I wanted to know more about the history of alchemy. I knew the stereotypes, the modern myths, but I wanted to know what real alchemists were doing in their labs.

✉️ Subscribe to the Newsletter!

Photo: mine

The Secrets of Alchemy by Dr. Lawrence Principe purported to answer this exact question and so I tore through that wondrous book, my face lit by screenglow. When I finished it, I dove into the footnote trail, seeking answers to further questions.

I've pored through a great number of books in the intervening years, and written a fair number of different blog posts on the subjects I discovered there. I met an array of different names: Ripley, Helmont, and Lull, different characters whose stories intermingled and wove a grand tale between the centuries on worn and precious parchment.

Did you know that the seventeenth century was the heyday for alchemy in Europe? Or that Isaac Newton was an alchemist. So was John Locke, in a way. The two were part of a circle of scientists, alchemists, doctors, and philosophers who would go on to found the Royal Society of London. So many famous names in history were there, bound up in the story of alchemy and its rise and fall from grace.

London in particular was a hotbed of alchemical interest at the time, as Germany had been in the decades before. All of Europe was abuzz with it. Yet, in all my reading, had there been no mention of the New World?

What about American Alchemists? Was there such a thing?

Library of Congress, Rare Book Room.
Photo: mine

That question would lead me right to him and to the realization that we'd already met. I'd forgotten his name, but Principe had introduced us and his colleague, Dr. William Newman, had penned the man's biography: George Starkey, a name that I will never forget again.

Born in Bermuda and educated as a doctor at Harvard, George Starkey became interested in alchemy early in life and so moved to London in his twenties to practice medicine and alchemy with England's best. At the time, alchemy, which was more akin to pharmacology today, was all the rage among the eager classes. Science was blossoming and so much was open to discovery.

It was with this understanding that Starkey came into the circle of Robert Boyle, John Locke, and Isaac Newton. Like Newton, Starkey is a rare breed among alchemists and among historical figures in general. You see, we have his personal notebooks, and so in addition to deciphering his published works, we get a glimpse behind the curtain into the sort of man he really was. Dr. Principe worked to translate those scribbled writings from their original Latin into English and in them we find a man working to untangle the mysteries of the universe, to puzzle out its causes and effects.

Starkey's Pseudonym. Library of Congress, Rare Book Room. Photo: mine

At the dawn of the modern age, Starkey and his cabal of conspirators wrote to each other as they quested to remake human knowledge. Starkey spent most of his free time beside his furnace, distilling various substances and trying to piece together the makeup of creation. He calculated mass lost to volatile vapors, discovered all manner of variously useful materials, and kept diligent notes that revealed a rather stubborn and quizzical nature. In a curious twist on the traditional method: rather than debate the nature of matter in the cloistered halls of the colleges, Starkey brought his inquiries directly to Nature herself, occasionally asking questions only to be refuted by the fire.

Aside from his successes making ice powder and specialist oils, Starkey described a new kind of "Philosophical Mercury" which he claims will lead him to his ultimate goal of making the Liquor Alkahest, a precursor to the philosopher's stone. He struggles with his work and his increasingly meager finances for years until on one page he writes:

Εύρηκα!

I remember reading that word, strangely Greek instead of Latin, in a coffeeshop one night. Mathematics taught me a few Greek letters and so I sounded out the word, knowing vaguely how the letters sound like their names. Eureka!

Photo: mine

On the next page we see a letter to his friend, Robert Boyle, recounting this discovery.

Now, to show you honor, [my friend] that I am an Englishman I will add a disaster.

Unfortunately, Starkey lost the results of this experiment, as the glassware flask that contained it broke and spilt its precious liquor into the coals. Reading this, I deflated in my chair right alongside him. His accounting of his life and his work is a baffling ride of success, of trial and error. It's all so very human.

On one page, Starkey wrote a set of prayers to God, and beside them a note to his future self: a plea, a reminder, to never drink so much wine at the tavern again.

[I swear,] I shall not game at any tavern for more than half a pint of wine at most nor be in the company of any gamester nor at play with any when I do play that I know to be a swearer or a vain person nor to stand by while they do play.

He notes later that he broke this promise.

A page of Starkey's notes, via Principe.
Photo: mine

It was through these pages, through the myriad descriptions of boiling and distilling this or that poisonous substance, through all the triumph and the failure, that I got to know Mr. Starkey not as a historical figure but as a man, a curious, insightful, and flawed man trying to understand the world.

Many of Starkey's letters to Robert Boyle survive. The two were friends and, for a time, Boyle was Starkey's student and patient. It was there, amid the pages of a particular letter to Boyle, that I was again captured and enthralled. In it, Starkey provides an update to his patron on the status of his experiments. Here was a man trying against the odds to follow in the footsteps of the Adepts in the same way all modern chemists follow in his.

It's in this letter that Starkey describes what would be, for him, a typical method of experiment.

While I was distilling, I took a drop to taste and in an instant it penetrated my tongue and at once made it bloody; and when by chance during its rectification I moved the candle nearby so that I might see whether any vapor was exhaling, the very light vapor took fire and burned with a truly stupendous spectacle.

Yet this experiment did more than burn his tongue and likely singe his eyebrows. Starkey truly believed that he was onto something momentous, although like many great discoveries, this one was accidental.

So when I wanted to determine whether it was combustible in a spoon, I poured out the first few drops falling [into the receiver] (because they contained some impurity that adhered to the neck of the retort) but being called by someone, I left the laboratory, since I did not want anyone to visit me there...

I left [the matter in] the spoon, and... left it alone until morning, by which time the liquor had exhaled, leaving behind a few drops of the greatest sweetness and greenness which evaporated when exposed to a moderate fire.

Good God, how I was filled with joy!

For me, the best part comes at the end. In a post-script, Starkey inquires about his friend's recent spat of bad health, but before that he closes with the following words. I've left the Latin in place this time because it's just as beautiful as the English translation.

Dederam volitanti Calamo altâ nocte quâ horâ plerique mortales dormire absolent prope Athanar meum.
Tuis studiosissimus, Georgius Stirke
♀ is Jan. ut puto 26, 1651

[My friend], I give to you my flying pen in the depth of night, when most mortals are wont to sleep, at my furnace.
Yours studiously, George Starkey
Friday, I think, January 26th, 1651*

It was in that moment, reading those words, that I had a new quest. I needed to see this letter. Not a translation on a page, but the real thing. There were no pictures of it in Principe's book, and so, armed with the manuscript number, I hurried to the Royal Society website, only to find that neither Starkey's notebooks nor this particular letter had been digitized. If I wanted to see them, I'd have to either go to London myself or work with the archivists to get them photographed.

One day I hope to visit the archives, but for now the latter would have to do.

I still visit the Timkin Museum, and the larger San Diego Art Museum right beside it, whenever I get the chance. When I do, I seek out works, like that of Mr. Bruegel, works old enough that it's possible Mr. Starkey would have seen them. We have no record that he ever did, of course, but to me that isn't really the point. What I feel, staring into those brush strokes is the same as when I read the pages of Starkey's letter: connection, with a history and with a man I've come to know.

One of the goals of the alchemists was transmutation, of base metals into gold. Another was eternal life. No one lives forever, but we all die two deaths: the first of the body, and the second when your name is said for the last time. Starkey never achieved the former, but the latter is within our power.

Thank you George Starkey. You have given me so much these past few years, and for that I am honored and so, here and now, I give to you my flying pen.

My thanks to Dr. Principe, Dr. Newman, and all the other authors I have read on this subject in recent years. It was you all who inspired me to dig deeper and eventually to inquire at the Royal Society. Thank you to the Royal Society, and to the hardworking archivists there who worked to preserve and image these letters, and to let me share them with the world.

Starkey's Letter To Boyle January 26 1651/2. Manuscript RB/3/5/70. Copyright: The Royal Society Of London
 
← scroll to see more →
Full-size image gallery →
Full-size image gallery →
Quotes from: Alchemical Laboratory Notebooks and Correspondence. P 49, 71, 72, 124
* This translation is my own.

items.title: What is Potential Energy, Really?
items.content_html:
As with seemingly every other man my age, I've taken up running to stay fit. Your metabolism slows as you age and what used to come for free with youth now takes time and deliberate effort to maintain. I don't care for the running, but it needs to be done.

The thing is: it does give me lots of idle time to think, just like a long walk. Both have become for me a form of meditation, a way to de-stress and to mull over complex ideas. I find that I think better when I'm moving, regardless of precisely how. Yet, near the end of every run my thoughts inevitably return to the same idea:

When will this be over? I want to be done.

Of course I want to complete my run, to go the distance I set for myself, but I also want, very badly, to do it in the most efficient way possible.

The Optimal Route

To end where you started, any route must go south for just as long as it goes north and the same goes for east and west. If you know it's three blocks west to get home and two blocks north then, because you're confined to the city grid, it doesn't matter what order you take those steps in. It's a quirk of city blocks that there are multiple shortest paths, but we'll come to that.1

E1=2U+3L E2=2U+3L E3=3U+3L+1D
Paths (1) and (2) take different routes but have the same total "effort" required to complete them and cover the same amount of total distance. It's only path (3) that differs. Why?

If you find that you need to add distance to your run as you go then you'll have to deviate from these ideal paths. To do that you need to use energy, more so than you would need to accomplish the ideal route. Of course you need energy to move your body in general but so long as we assume that you always intend to eventually go back home, and that your speed is constant, the energy to go from here to there is fixed by your current position along the ideal path, and thus already accounted for. The energy required to traverse that path can't change because that would require the path to get longer, and that means it wouldn't be the ideal path anymore. Thus, what can change is the amount of energy you use to get home beyond that fixed amount.

Etotal=Eideal+Eadditions

We can arrive at a formal definition by renaming a few things. If we call the shortest, ideal route a geodesic, then this added energy is defined as whatever energy is required to deviate from a geodesic. We call this "potential energy" (V). If we rename the energy required to move along the geodesic the "kinetic energy" (T) then what we have is the familiar equation from elementary physics.2

E=T+V

Crucially this potential energy is only expended to deviate from the ideal path, not to relax back toward it—that's just the process of following the new shortest path. In the (1)/(3) split in our diagram above, the energy is expended along the path of the green arrow. From there the path back is fully determined. One consequence of this is that, in our example, added blocks always come in pairs. Whatever additional city blocks you traverse away from your destination must eventually be retraced if you are to get home.

Now these are not the typical definitions of these terms that you find in elementary physics, because in that context, kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Here we've discussed it as simply the energy required to reach a given destination. However these are two sides of the same coin. Throwing a ball from A to B causes the ball to move. If we don't know where the ball will land (i.e. we don't know the value of B), then we can define the kinetic energy to be the energy of motion and use that to compute the value of B. If we know the values of A and B already, then the kinetic energy is just the energy required to reach B from A. These are the same argument given two different framings.

Keep in mind it doesn't matter that a real ball won't end its journey mid-air, but it doesn't end it's journey when it hits the ground either. It's still riding on the moving Earth.

✉️ Subscribe to the Newsletter!

One obvious complaint you may have about my city-block example is that it's wrong. The ideal path between my starting point and ending point is a straight line! That's Euclid's first postulate from geometry! It's the very definition of what a straight line even is, right?

Isn't all this just a bit silly?

And you'd be entirely correct, kind of.

The thing is, you can't run as the crow flies, at least I can't. Confined to the ground, such a straight line path isn't an option. This is an important restriction because it allows us to redefine what the word distance even means. We will come out of that discussion with something much more powerful than we might first expect. To do that I have one question we must answer:

What's the distance from Rome to Edinburgh?

A clever reader might want to know which units I want them to use, but the cleverest of you might instead ask me, for whom? For a car the journey is about 1,545 miles; for a plane it's 1,002. For the Roman Emperor Hadrian it is, rather famously, undefined.

Image credit: Apple Maps
Image credit: Great Circle Mapper
Image credit: Wikimedia Commons

This is all to say that the concept of distance is not independent of the constraints of motion. If we define distance in this way, then we get something called a metric which is our ruler to measure space. Euclid gave us one kind of ruler: the Euclidean Metric defined by the familiar Pythagorean Theorem.

c=a2+b2
The Euclidean Metric

However we can also define a metric that works for our city blocks. This one looks quite different from the usual measure we use and it results in a radically different notion of length. In principle though, lots of functions can be used as metrics and each has its own consequences. The point is that there's no limit to how you define the idea of length.

c=|a−b|
The Taxi Cab Metric

Why are we talking about this though? What does any of this have to do with potential energy? That is where we arrive at one of the most important discoveries in all of physics.

Bending the Grid

Once you understand that the notion of distance depends on the properties of motion and how you draw your grid, you find yourself where Einstein was after 1905, after his first major breakthrough but before he reformulated gravity.

Anyone who's taken high school or introductory college physics knows that Newton taught us that gravity is a force that pulls objects to the ground. That idea was later generalized to the idea that objects live in something called a gravitational field and that field imparts the object with gravitational potential energy.

Einstein realized however that this idea was overbuilt. Instead, he found a different way to understand how gravity works. To see how let's take a step back. Imagine a grid, but a bent one, where the lines are warped. By definition, those lines mark out equal distance so even when they're warped we still say that they are the same distance apart. To see how this is possible, imagine that instead the paper itself is warped and the lines are straight along that warping. You can kind of see this if you squint at the image below.

Warped lines or warped paper? Is there a difference?

The ball in the image above has moved along the straightest possible path, it's just that the lines defining straightness are bent, so the ball seems to curve. This, in a nutshell, is gravity. Massive objects like the Earth and Sun bend the very grid of space and time. They, in a sense, redefine what it means to move in a straight line.

Under this formulation, there was no need for gravitational potential energy at all. The Earth doesn't pull you down. You want to fall toward it because spacetime is curved. It's actually the opposite: the Earth is preventing you from falling!

This wonderful lecture goes through an excellent derivation of this idea that I encourage you to watch. It opened my eyes to a lot of this. Consider Newton's First Law:

A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, unless it is acted upon by a force.

The key insight for those of you still rightfully confused by all this is that usually we define what an object does (move in a line) and then say happens to it (it's acted on by a force). This is only possible because we arrive at the problem with a pre-formulated idea of what a straight line is. Instead we can flip it and then define what a straight line is by what an object does when there's no force on it! In the first instance we define straightness and derive forces. In the second, we eliminate the forces and define whatever happens next as a straight line. So, if the object seems to bend towards the Earth, then that's a straight line. It has to be!

We've moved from imposing a definition to observing one. In a sense we take a step back and watch what nature does, rather than telling it what it should do. In doing so we package two concepts into one and gain predictive power.

But enough about gravity. We were talking about running, right?

Closer to Home

If you follow the city grid on a run, then you're using some variant of the Taxi-Cab Metric to measure distance, and you're constrained by the physics of that metric. I've wondered why the path back home doesn't seem to matter, but it's because of the metric. In Taxi-Cab geometry there are multiple shortest paths. In Euclidean geometry there is only one. No path directly home will affect your total distance. And so, if you need that extra half-mile, you can only get it by running away from where you started, so long as the blocks are essentially the same size. So long as you are retracing blocks, you follow a straight line, a geodesic, back home. Use up some potential energy though, add a single block, and notice you'll actually have added two once you get back. Technically the second block was a geodesic though, but it all still counts.

1 Assuming of course that the E/W and N/S blocks are of equal length. If they aren't then we actually fastrack to the discussion of curved coordinates in later sections.
2 No I have no idea why T and V were the chosen names for these. Susskind in his class didn't either, but neither of us have looked it up.

items.title: Friendship is an Exponential Function
items.content_html:
What allows you to make friends and to keep them? Being a social person helps with making friends, surely. As does putting in the effort to be a good friend. But I'm sure we've all had the experience of wanting to become friends with someone, but yet it never really happens. Maybe there's never the time. Maybe you're too far apart, and I mean that literally.

This is something I've observed over time, as friends move around and as people's lives grow, evolve, and change: the total friendship between two people evolves as a function of distance.

I think this is how we want or expect friendship to behave.

This means that two people, given the inclination to become friends, will see their friendship improve and decay based on their physical distance from each other—how far they live from each other. I think this makes intuitive sense. Two people who live together obviously see each other more than two people who live a continent apart. Yet what is surprising is that this function is not linear.

Friendships, in my experience, are strengthened not by planned time together, but by accidental happenstance and the unplanned ability to simply spend time in the same place. If you live next door to a friend, spending time together is easy. Outside of your home, that friend is your easiest option for social interaction. You can share meals, woes, gossip, and even just yell over the fence to each other. That closeness is not a function of your effort to connect, but precisely because of the lack of effort you both needed to expend!

Given suitable places to go, a coffee, dinner, or beer with friends nearby becomes a text message away.

Beer at Ould Sod?

Friendship falls off quickly with distance, then that descent slows down.

In business-speak: there is very little friction here. Again think of a friendship within a household. You don't schedule wine with dinner. You just see if your friend or partner wants some, then open the bottle. The need to schedule, especially with a calendar, is the sign of a friendship's formality. It's the sign that physical distance has intruded on your shared lives.

Yet, I assume none of this is surprising. The important thing I've discovered is that this function of distance is not linear as I said. We expect that moving a little further away would have a proportional effect on the friendship. In practice though, it's exponential.

This means that friendship, given no additional effort, will decay much faster than you think. Moving a block away is worse than being next door by a surprising amount. Moving across town marks the end of an era. Sure, given time and deliberate effort (and lots of calendars) you can overcome the barrier of distance. The internet has helped here too, but scheduled time and video calls are no basis for the same friendships that occur naturally in backyards, on doorsteps, or at nearby restaurants, coffeeshops, and bar counters.

There's an old meme:

Photo: mine

Half the reason folks romanticize college is because it's the last time most folks lived in dense, walkable neighborhoods focused on providing community during plentiful off-hours.

I've been lucky enough to be able to live in a vibrant, walkable, and third-place abundant neighborhood for over a decade. What's more I've been luckier still in that many of my friends live within walking distance. I grew up in a small neighborhood with several kids down the street to play with. In a way I still have that, for now.

What it means though is that to be nearby is to be part of a group of friends who are just simply closer than my other friends, even if we weren't all that close to begin with. It's just easier to hang out, easier to spend time, and friendship, if anything, is a function of time spent together. That time is a function of effort, of shared interest, and importantly the exponential of distance.

items.title: Because it Speaks in Words
items.content_html:
There is a difference between knowing something, and truly understanding it. I think we've all had those moments, the ones where a truth you learned a long time ago really sits with you for the first time. It rests in your mind and stretches out, finally showing off the great expanse of nuance hidden deep within.

Photo: mine.

Most nights when you happen to spy the Moon, Jupiter, and Venus sitting in a line in the sky, you see them as the dots beside a crescent that they are. Yet sometimes, when framed amid the sunset sky above the wisps of silver cloud, you see them differently. You realize in that moment that you, your great-grandparents, Julius Caesar, and Aristotle all saw this same sky. It has always been for us. We know so much about Jupiter and Venus today, yet no human eye has ever seen more than you're seeing now.

I think we are all, in this time, realizing the true power of words and what they mean, not to those who speak, but to those who listen.

The Power of Stories

It was Eugene Wigner who famously wrote about the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the Natural Sciences, the empirical fact that advanced math is eerily accurate at predicting the behavior of nature, so much so that, for me, it can seem like mathematics is perhaps the true language that nature speaks.

However, as children, we do not grow up with an innate understanding of complex mathematics, of this foundational language of nature. Instead we are all born with the innate desire to hear and to tell stories, of ourselves, of others, and of the world around us. Our well-known cognitive biases push us to accept stories that rhyme over those that do not, and believe the people we speak to. That last one is particularly important in this age because there are simply so many words out there ready to be believed.

Stories are how we share information and how we've warned, cast out, and praised each other for millenia. We tell stories, to ourselves and to others, about why we are successful (or not) and why others might be (or not). We moralize disease, in part perhaps because a moral story is easier to bear than the sheer randomness of a chaotic world. Our minds work to make sense of the world by finding patterns. As those patterns interweave and become cohesive narratives, a story emerges to explain the where and why. These stories are so critical to our understanding of the world that we hold on to them, make them part of our selves, and when they break down they can break the self too. In the end, all we have of the world and the only truth we know first-hand, are the stories we tell ourselves.

We communicate those stories, to ourselves and to others, with gestures, actions, and most importantly with words. That makes those words perhaps the most powerful force in human society. They are the fundamental interaction that holds our world together. It's the words from the past that we reach for as some justification or authority. It's words of the famous and the clever that we laud or reject. Even Mathematics, this jewel of the modern world, is communicated and taught in words. To our storied minds, these atoms of thought are everything.

Ulysses and the Sirens. John William Waterhouse
via Wikimedia Commons

Disinformation and misinformation have been rampant in the past, but never before has there been a world filled so chaotically with so many clamoring voices. The Ancient Greeks warned of Sirens and their terrible, entrancing songs, yet today sirens sound in our ears and on our eyes every moment of every single day.

However today, we have also come into a new thing, a step function in our communication. In this time we humans are not the only one who is talking. This is not because we are some perfect specimen of wordcraft, or that another species could not do what we do, but because our chosen, crafted interlocutor is not a mind like ours. It is a device which has no notion of truth or of morality. It is a parrot, who imitates our speech but does not understand it. It does not learn, and it cannot. Yet we still can, and we will learn what it tells us, regardless of its truth.

Words Without a Mind

Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are a type of machine learning algorithm that have been around a long time. Random Forests are another. Both are very good at sifting through swaths of noise looking for the signal. SVMs and Random Forests help identify disease incidence in large populations, and find novel ways to identify genetic causes of complex conditions. Techniques like these were spreading in academia and industry a decade ago. I remember when Apple released a drag-and-drop app to help developers build simple models for recommendation systems! This stuff has been around for a long time.

Yet, if that's true, why did it take Large Language Models (LLMs) to break into mainstream consciousness? People had been hammering on the idea of rebranding Machine Learning as Artificial Intelligence for years, but these days LLMs are synonymous with AI while other techniques aren't. True, modern LLMs are impressive technically, but is that the reason? Or is the reason totally distinct from technology? Perhaps we call LLMs intelligent, perhaps we adopted them in a frenetic rush, and perhaps we fear them most not because they are particularly good machine learning algorithms, but because, at long last, they do not speak in vectors or in numbers, but because they speak in words and words are our domain.

Ulysses and the Sirens. John William Waterhouse
via Wikimedia Commons

I think back to a cognitive bias I listed above: that we tend to believe the people we are speaking to. No other machine learning technique, no other AI, has ever spoken to us, sounded so much like another mind. At every opportunity when technology has enabled new forms of communication: books, pamphlets, letters, emails, instant messenger, text messaging, we have always used those tools to seek out others like ourselves and to share and listen to new stories. Those stories used to correlate roughly with some level of truth about the world, if even about a single interpretation of it. Now we have language statistically built to sound genuine, and yet its speaker has no mind or experience to convey. Still, we believe so deeply in the power of words that many of us have preferred this plausible-sounding make-believe to reality.

Left Wanting

There is evidence that perhaps LLMs, unlike social media, will help push us to the center—to the statistical average—and if LLMs were somehow guaranteed to only be trained on human-generated data forever, perhaps this would be true. However as we further diverge the words we see from any objective meaning, both in human communication and in the words written by our new AI chatbots, this situation will not be stable for long.

Ultimately though, what's important is not that we have built tools to generate digital text. What is important is that, like processed food and sugar, our long-ingrained biological need to share and hear stories is being hijacked and used by technology. Ascribe whatever values to that you wish, the morality is not my point. Humans have looked out at the stars and wondered why: why we live and die, and whether this universe was made for us, and whether we belong within it for millenia. Those questions remain, save now we have the ability to trust in a voice that tells us precisely what we want to hear. We filled a caloric need with cheap candy, shelf-stable cupcakes, and soda. These are convenient things, good in moderation, but still they can hurt us and we're still struggling to solve the problems they created. Today we may be filling an emotional need as well, functioning as the scheming court vizier that whispers sweet and comfortable truths. Yet unlike the stereotype, this vizier does not scheme. It has no mind and no goal save to please, yet we wish so deeply to be pleased.

The Uncanny Valley
Masahiro Mori and Karl MacDorman

This need comes deeply ingrained in us and will be impossible to fill. It is part of the Human Condition. Perhaps, given time, this new kind of statistically-driven language will find itself deep within the unforgiving well of the Uncanny Valley. We shall see. No doubt the Sirens seemed convincing for a time. As a gas-station pastry is no substitute for a good and hearty meal, the words of prediction engines are but vain and fickle things, lovely in the ear perhaps but hardly satisfying to the soul.

For millenia words have been a proxy for connection with another mind, today that link is severed but the need in us remains and there is only so long that one can fill a void with empty calories. We retain our position as the only being in the Universe who can tell their own stories and who can be said to learn and share the truth. The Font of Knowledge still begins and ends with us and The Odessy of Finding Truth is a lonely one, cast as we are amid the stormy waters of the world, even as there are many clamorous, seductive voices calling to us from the distant shore.
